name: Froggy Hop
desc: The bouncy 8-bit loop from the Frog vs Toad game — now with pad/lead automation, per-instrument envelopes and crash/clap accents.

name: Cinematic
desc: A ~2-minute epic in A minor — intro, theme, bridge, climax and outro with strings, horn, brass and arps, swelling into the climax via automation.

name: Techno
desc: A ~2-minute 128 BPM journey — intro, groove, build, drop, breakdown and a bigger second drop, with riser automation and backbeat claps into each drop.

name: Neon Drive
desc: An original 80s synth-pop song at 120 BPM — verse, chorus, bridge and a soaring final chorus, with a sequenced arp, lush swelling pad, synth-bass slides and a proper melodic hook.

name: Deep Vacuum
desc: A 132 BPM techno track for the Space Miner game — sparse vacuum-drone intros/outros build into hard-hitting drops via riser arps and crash transitions, with bitcrushed lead stabs, chorused pads and a tightened master EQ/compressor for a deeper, punchier sound.

name: Orbital Standby
desc: Lobby music for the Space Miner game — 96 BPM, D minor, two minutes of wide sine pad, a halfsine bell hook and a broken pulse arp over rim and shaker. Written to loop: it swells to a wide middle section and recedes to exactly the pad-and-bass texture it opened with, so bar 48 hands back to bar 1 without a seam.

name: The Fitting Bay
desc: Shop music for the Space Miner game — a 118 BPM shuffle in F major, bright and major where the lobby is wide and minor, so walking in is an audible event. Plucky pulse lead with a diatonic third under it, bouncing root-fifth-octave bass, till-drawer chimes, and a light rim-and-shaker kit that thins out over the last four bars.

name: Neon Cathedral
desc: A 2-minute symphonic/techno hybrid at 128 BPM — intro, build, drop, breakdown and a key-change climax before the outro. Six tracks (sine pad, square arp lead, FM brass stabs, triangle sub-bass, and two rhythm kits) showcase nearly every feature: per-note bend/vibrato/arpeggio/portamento/bitcrush/duty-cycle, ADSR + filter envelopes, FM synthesis, volume/pan/delay/reverb automation curves, per-track Delay/Chorus/Reverb sends, Compressor, Bitcrush and Tremolo inserts, plus master EQ, compressor, parallel compression, kick-triggered sidechain ducking and a touch of master bitcrush.

name: Rust Foundry
desc: Industrial metal at 140 BPM — a downtuned E-phrygian chug riff double-tracked hard left and right, a ring-modulated machine drone, an FM alarm lead and two kits. Built around how hard things are hit and where they sit: ghost snares against a full backbeat, hats accented on the beat, tom fills that walk across the stereo field, and scrap percussion clanking off-grid. Bitcrush as distortion, a mid-scooped master, parallel compression and kick-triggered ducking.

name: Rasterline
desc: A 132 BPM C64 pastiche in A minor, written to exercise the SID voices rather than to hide them. A saw+triangle bass jumps octaves instead of sweeping a filter; the chord voice is one held note per bar carrying its whole triad, arpeggiated at 50 Hz so it reads as a chord rather than a fast melody; and the lead is hard sync with its ratio swept, entering at bar 9 once the ostinato has established itself. Sixteen bars of i-VI-III-VII, which is a progression precisely because a SID has three voices and the chord has to be implied.

name: Three Voices
desc: Rasterline under the SID's actual constraint: same key, tempo, progression and melody, but three tonal channels and no drum kit, because that is what a 6581 has. Every voice does double duty — the lead puts the chord down and picks it back up in its own rests, the bass drops an octave and cuts short for a kick, and a single pitched noise channel is both hat and snare. Meant to be A/B'd against Rasterline: the music is identical, so what you hear is the budget.

name: Inventio
desc: J.S. Bach's Invention No. 13 in A minor, BWV 784, arranged for three SID voices. An invention has two voices of equal weight in the middle of the keyboard and no bass at all, so the third voice is built from Bach's own lower line: the note it is sounding on each beat, moved into the bass register and given the octave-drop kick a chip uses instead of a drum. Every pitch here is Bach's — nothing harmonic was invented, which is what keeps the counterpoint from being second-guessed. Notes taken from the Humdrum kern encoding of the Bach-Gesellschaft edition by David Huron and Craig Stuart Sapp, rather than transcribed from memory: a cover of a known piece may be many things, but not nearly right.

name: Vertical Blank
desc: An original 128 BPM piece in D minor, named after the interrupt the whole thing hangs off: the chord voice is a narrow 25% pulse arpeggiated at 50 Hz — one step per PAL vertical blank — so a triad costs one channel instead of three. A saw+triangle bass runs unbroken sixteenths, alternating root and octave rather than sweeping a filter, and the lead is swept PWM with vibrato on anything long enough to hold. i-III-VI-VII for the theme, with a major dominant in the B section for the harmonic-minor lift. Four voices, one more than a 6581: the classic trick was to multiplex drums and bass through a single channel a raster apart, and this engine picks its waveform per track rather than per note, so the drums get their own. Percussion is one pitched noise channel and is deliberately monophonic — a real voice cannot play a kick and a hat at once. Written to be A/B'd against a real SID: it is an idiom, not a cover, so what you are comparing is the synthesis.

name: Canone
desc: J.S. Bach's Invention No. 8 in F major, BWV 779, for three SID voices. The first four bars are a strict canon at the octave one bar apart — 34 of 34 notes exact — and it loosens from there, which is why the bass, derived from the lower staff, spends the opening chasing the melody a bar behind. Bright and in 3/4: a triple metre has no half-bar, so the octave-drop kick lands on the downbeat alone rather than twice a bar.

name: Dodici
desc: J.S. Bach's Invention No. 12 in A major, BWV 783, for three SID voices. Twelve in both senses: the twelfth invention, in 12/8. The beat is a dotted quarter rather than an eighth, so the derived bass pumps in four to the bar and not in twelve — get that wrong and the song is a machine gun. The lilt is Bach's; the octave-hopping bass under it is the chip's.

name: Sinfonia Quarta
desc: J.S. Bach's Sinfonia No. 4 in D minor, BWV 790, for three SID voices — and the one arrangement here that required no invention at all. A sinfonia already has three real voices, so they map straight onto the three channels with nothing left over: no derived bass, no percussion, not even a stolen kick, because the kick trick destroys the note it lands on and that is acceptable on a line I derived but vandalism on a line Bach wrote. Same key area and metre as Inventio, so an A/B between them is about voice structure and nothing else.

name: Air
desc: J.S. Bach's Air from the third orchestral suite, BWV 1068, for three SID voices — the real voice-stealing problem. The Air is in four parts and a 6581 has three channels, so Violin II and the viola share the third: one note carrying an arpeggio that alternates between their two pitches fifty times a second, which is exactly what a chip's arpeggio is for. Both pitches are Bach's; only the alternation is the chip's. In D major, read off the notes rather than the title — 'on the G String' is Wilhelmj's violin transposition to C, and this is the orchestral original. Note values are doubled so the melody's thirty-seconds land exactly on the app's lattice, which means the bar counter reads two for every written bar; the markers give the written numbers back.
